The blind f_+ sends inr u to inr u, but ours sends it to inr ★. These are not definitionally equal. The two pointed maps are identified by a pointed homotopy, by case split. The functor laws are transported from ours. The functor (−)_÷ is ours by refl.

The book leaves the pointing path of Ω k implicit. The blind statement uses ch. 4's loops_map_point, the inverse of the explicit loop_conjugate_unit. Ours (module 616) uses the inverse of the J-defined loop_conj_unit. The two 2-paths are identified by path induction and a 3-dimensional coherence at refl. This coherence uses the naturality of concat_1p, λ_refl = ρ_refl from module 281 and the typal Jβ. Then the functor laws are transported from ours.
The actions on objects and arrows are the same, and the functor data are equal by refl. The blind laws are refl, as ours are.

The objects, arrows and identities agree by refl. The composites differ only in the square proof, which is a proposition. Thus the identity functors in both directions form a strict isomorphism. Isomorphisms correspond, and our univalence transfers.

The statement blind_xca_wildprecat_of_wildprecats (λ, ρ, α for composition of wild functors) is bridged from module 644. The statement blind_xca_wildprecat_pentagon asks for some λ, ρ, α with pentagon fillers for all quadruples of wild functors. It is derived as bridge_xca_wildprecat_pentagon. Here λ and ρ are as before, and α is the translation of our functor_assoc_yoneda (module 693). The fillers are transported from wild_precat_yoneda_pentagon (modules 692–694, arbitrary wild C_4) by bridge_pentagon_transfer. This transfer is generic in the associator, because ap of the record translation preserves concatenation. The blind left side is bracketed (a1·a2)·a3, and ours is a1·(a2·a3). The blind statement lets the associator be chosen. Thus it is no deviation that our pentagon uses functor_assoc_yoneda and not functor_assoc.
